payload.title: What Are the Javanese Wedding Traditions You Did Not Know?
payload.audience: Couples in their 30s interested in destination weddings and luxury experiences, AUD 150k+ budget
payload.reader: An Australian couple in their 30s with a generous budget, often with a Javanese-Indonesian partner or parent, who want to understand each Javanese custom in the order it happens, which ones belong to the palace (Yogyakarta or Solo) and which to families everywhere, and what it takes to marry legally in Java or Bali or to bring the customs home to an Australian wedding.
payload.goal: Read the free Wedded Wonderland digital magazine (primary CTA); secondary, in-context invitation to speak with a Wedded Advisor placed straight after the legal section.
payload.service_link: /magazine (primary, UTM-tagged); /wonderland-concierge (secondary, UTM-tagged, after the legal section)
payload.angle: A Javanese wedding is a sequence, not a list: we walk 12 customs in the order families hold them, from nontoni and lamaran months before to sungkeman on the day, separate what the Kraton Yogyakarta records as royal practice from what families commonly do, show how Solo and Yogyakarta styles differ in the bride's paes ageng, source each from palace, UNESCO, Indonesian government and academic pages (saying 'often told' where they are thin), and end with what Australians need to marry legally in Java or Bali as at November 2026. Deeper and more ordered than the Indonesian overview and page-one listicles, which stop at siraman, midodareni and panggih.
must_include: One early framing line: customs vary by family, faith and region; palace accounts describe royal practice, not every wedding
Customs in chronological order, grouped Before the day / The day and after, each numbered
Panggih broken into its named steps in order (H3s or a numbered list), covering every step the old page named
Solo (Surakarta) and Yogyakarta styles compared for paes ageng, only where sourced
UNESCO Indonesian Batik 2009 with its marriage line; Gamelan 2021 only if UNESCO text mentions weddings

Legal section for Australians marrying in Java or Bali (same religion, CNI, KUA or Civil Registry, recognition in Australia, Smartraveller level 2 with Papua level 3 areas, Java and Bali unaffected), 'as at November 2026', check fees with the embassy and registry
Javanese-Australian weddings at home: how couples hold siraman, sungkeman or panggih in Australia, with respect notes (ask the families, use a juru paes or family elders for rites)
FAQ of 5 to 6 questions covering the old page's question set (main rituals, panggih, what the bride wears, siraman, religious or not, traditional vs modern)
Reciprocal link to /expert-advice/indonesian-wedding-traditions near the top and in the legal section

tradition_plan.note: Planner (wedding-planner-sme) runs batch A and batch B in parallel, scratch folders 02-research/batch-a and 02-research/batch-b, 15 min HARD by the clock, save after every 3 facts, no extra sourcing rounds. Re-use first: re-check (live fetch, title and date) before re-use; do not re-source what the Indonesian pack already holds. Preferred new sources: kratonjogja.id, kratonsolo / Kasunanan Surakarta official pages, warisanbudaya.kemdikbud.go.id, kebudayaan.kemdikbud.go.id, dpad.jogjaprov.go.id, budaya.jogjaprov.go.id, ich.unesco.org, museums (Museum Sonobudoyo, Museum Batik), peer-reviewed journals (Widyaparwa, Jantra, Garuda-indexed). Never competitor wedding sites, Wikipedia, lifestyle magazines. Unsourced: 'often told', no meanings stated as fact, no [[VERIFY]] marker.
tradition_plan.count: 12 customs plus the legal section (batch A: 6 customs; batch B: 6 customs plus legal)

weton or date-setting by the Javanese calendar as one line only if sourced
what peningsetan means (binding or tying) and what the groom's family brings (cloth, ring, foods) as items, never amounts
difference from seserahan if sourced

batch_A.tradition: Pasang tarub and bleketepe (decorating the bride's home)
facts_to_source: tarub (temporary decorated roof or entrance) and bleketepe (woven coconut leaves) put up by the bride's father, if sourced

both bride and groom bathed, purification inward and outward
seven-spring water as ROYAL practice only
who pours (parents and elders), and ngerik afterwards
dodol dhawet (selling dawet) only if sourced
name from bidadari and its meaning

batch_A.tradition: Ijab or akad nikah (the marriage contract, in Muslim families)
facts_to_source: ijab qobul as the core rite that makes the marriage
wali, two witnesses, mahar named without amounts (KHI)

framing: most Javanese weddings are Muslim but not all; Christian and other ceremonies follow their own rite
order of steps from the Kraton page
balangan gantal (betel-leaf throw)
wiji dadi / ngidak endog (egg step) and the bride washing the groom's foot
sindur binayang (sindur cloth walk led by the bride's parents)
timbang or pangkon (father's lap) only if sourced
kacar-kucur / tampa kaya (coins and grains)
dhahar klimah / dulangan (feeding each other)

batch_B.tradition: LEGAL: marrying in Java or Bali as Australians
facts_to_source: DFAT cannot advise on Indonesian requirements; recognised religion; same religion under Law 1/1974

recognition in Australia (1995) and that an overseas marriage cannot be registered in Australia (Smartraveller)
Smartraveller level 2 overall, level 3 Papua Pegunungan and Papua Tengah; Java and Bali not in a higher area; missions in Jakarta, Bali, Surabaya (East Java), Makassar
option: marry legally in Australia, hold the Javanese rites in Java or Bali
fees: 'check with the embassy and the registry', as at November 2026
no Advisor help with legal or religious paperwork implied
